articles.title: REITs come of age: 29 schemes and a seventh listing on the PSX
articles.excerpt: Real estate investment trusts are giving developers a new source of money and investors a way into property. Where the market stands in 2026.

sources.title: ProPakistani, "SECP approves PSX listing of Naya Nazimabad Apartments REIT", 18 August 2026

articles.body:
For most investors in Pakistan, putting money into property has meant buying a plot or a flat. Real estate investment trusts (REITs) offer another way: buying units in a fund that owns or develops property, traded like shares.

Where the market stands

According to a report on the approval of the Naya Nazimabad Apartments REIT in August 2026, Pakistan has 29 registered REIT schemes, of which six are listed on the Pakistan Stock Exchange. The Naya Nazimabad Apartments REIT is set to become the seventh.

A developmental REIT

The Naya Nazimabad scheme is a closed-end developmental REIT under the REIT Regulations, 2022 — it raises money to build, rather than only to own finished buildings. The public offering covers 44.06 million units, 15% of the scheme, with 75% offered to institutional and high-net-worth investors and 25% to retail investors through book building. The SECP described it as the 13th public offering it had approved in 2026.

Why it matters for construction

  • Developers get access to money from many investors, not just bank loans or advance payments from buyers.
  • Buyers can see a project funded before it is sold off-plan, which can reduce the risk of stalled schemes.
  • Investors can own a share of property with smaller sums, and sell their units on the exchange.
  • Transparency improves, because listed REITs must report regularly to the regulator and investors.

Things to keep in mind

REIT units can fall in value, and developmental REITs carry construction risk. As with any investment, investors should read the offering document and take professional advice.

REITs and tokenisation were on the agenda of the PROPTECH Convention at Build Asia 2026. Read what the conference covered.

articles.title: Public–private partnerships in Pakistan: the P3A, its projects and how firms take part
articles.excerpt: The PPP Authority has moved under the Privatisation Division, and motorways are among the projects being prepared as PPPs. How the framework works, which projects are live and where private firms come in.

sources.title: Profit by Pakistan Today, "Public Private Partnership Authority's administrative control shifted to Privatisation Division", 13 May 2026
Profit by Pakistan Today, "Govt moves to award Rs205 billion Kharian-Rawalpindi Motorway to FWO", 25 June 2026
ProPakistani, "Construction Starting Date Announced for New Motorway", 22 September 2026

articles.body:
Alongside the PSDP and lender-funded schemes, some of Pakistan’s large projects are being prepared as public–private partnerships (PPPs): projects where a private company finances, builds and runs an asset under a concession.

How the framework works

The Public Private Partnership Authority (P3A) was set up under the PPP Authority Act, 2017. It provides the legal framework and helps federal agencies structure, develop and procure PPP projects. Key points, as reported by Profit in May 2026:

  • Since a 2020 amendment, the P3A handles “Qualified” projects directly; other projects can go ahead with approval from the implementing agency’s principal accounting officer.
  • The P3A board approves projects that give the public sector value for money while staying financially viable for private investors.
  • Private firms may submit unsolicited proposals for projects the government has not identified but considers suitable for a PPP.
  • In May 2026, administrative control of the P3A moved from the Planning Division to the Privatisation Division, with the stated aim of widening private participation in infrastructure.

Projects in the pipeline

ProjectSizeStatus (2026)
Kharian–Rawalpindi Motorway (M-13)117 km, Rs203.32bn (ECNEC, April 2026)Build-operate-transfer; viability gap of over Rs40bn to be met by the federal government
M-6 sections I and II, Hyderabad–Nawabshah120 km, Rs151bn combinedTendering from 6 Nov 2026; concession award targeted for 4 Feb 2027; ADB as transaction adviser

The M-13 cost has more than doubled from Rs96 billion in January 2022, after the road was upgraded from four to six lanes. ECNEC directed international competitive bidding, but in June 2026 Profit, citing Dawn, reported that the P3A board had backed, in principle, a negotiated award to the Frontier Works Organisation, subject to federal cabinet approval (not yet given as of that report).

How private firms take part

Our observations:

  • As concessionaires or sponsors, bidding for tendered PPP sections such as M-6 I and II, or bringing an unsolicited proposal.
  • As subcontractors and suppliers to whoever wins, for materials, plant, tolling systems and maintenance.
  • What to watch: the M-13 case shows that the procurement route for a PPP project can change after it has been approved.

articles.title: Apni Chhat Apna Ghar: over 100,000 homes built with Punjab’s interest-free loans
articles.excerpt: By June 2026 Punjab’s housing programme had completed 100,633 houses with more than Rs208 billion in interest-free loans. What it means for building-material demand.

sources.title: The News, "2,000 families being provided free residential plots: minister", 12 March 2026
The News, "‘Apni Chhat, Apna Ghar’ project: 100,633 houses complete, minister told", 3 June 2026
The Express Tribune, "Applicants await ‘Apni Chhat Apna Ghar’ loans", 25 August 2026

articles.body:
Punjab’s Apni Chhat Apna Ghar (“my roof, my home”) programme lends families money, interest-free, to build a house on their own plot, which is pledged as security. Because each family builds its own home, in our view much of the money goes into local purchases of cement, bricks, steel and fittings.

Progress in 2026

Figures given to the Punjab Housing Minister, Bilal Yasin, by the Punjab Housing and Town Planning Agency (PHATA) show how fast the programme moved in the first half of the year:

IndicatorMarch 2026June 2026
Houses completed83,330100,633
Houses under construction45,42532,412
Families given loans131,680over 156,000
Loans providedover Rs183 billionover Rs208 billion

In March 2026 the programme had more than 1.9 million registrations and over 1.135 million applications, and Rs8.4 billion had been repaid. In June the minister said the government would fund interest-free loans for another 100,000 families in the coming fiscal year.

A companion scheme, Apni Zameen Apna Ghar, was providing free residential plots to 2,000 families, according to the minister in March 2026.

What this means for materials demand

By our own arithmetic, about 17,300 houses were completed between the March and June updates — well over 5,000 a month. A few observations follow:

  • Small, scattered buyers: loans of up to Rs1.5 million each (as reported in Vehari) go to individual families across the province, so demand reaches district dealers and shops rather than big contractors.
  • Basic materials first: cement, bricks, steel bars, roofing, doors, windows, wiring and sanitary fittings make up most of a modest single-family house.
  • Room for efficient methods: standard designs and faster building systems could help families build within a fixed loan; see our article on light-gauge steel framing.

What to watch

The Express Tribune reported in August 2026 that applicants in Vehari whose loans were approved between January and June 2026 were still waiting for their first instalment. Demand from the programme depends on the money arriving on time.

For the national picture, read Pakistan’s housing gap in numbers. Material makers and dealers serving the housing market meet at Build Asia 2027, 18–20 March 2027 at the Karachi Expo Centre. You can register to visit.

articles.title: 7,000 MW on the rooftops: how solar is reshaping building design
articles.excerpt: Net-metered solar grew 37-fold in six years. Roofs, structures and wiring now have to be designed for panels from day one.

sources.title: ProPakistani, "Pakistan's solar boom reaches 7,000 MW as govt moves to replace net metering", 17 July 2026

articles.body:
Pakistan’s rooftops have changed faster than almost anyone expected. Solar generation under net metering grew from 190 MW in FY2020 to about 6,978 MW by FY2026 — nearly 37 times in six years — according to figures presented by Syed Faizan Ali, Energy Adviser to the Power Division.

Why it happened

The same presentation set out the drivers: electricity tariffs rose about 140% between FY2021 and FY2025, while the rupee lost about 75% of its value and imported solar panel prices fell by about 60%. For many homes and businesses, generating their own power became the obvious choice.

The rules are changing

Under the Prosumer Regulations 2026, which took effect on 8 February 2026, new consumers move to net billing: electricity they export to the grid is paid at a lower reference price rather than credited one-for-one. Consumers with 2015 net-metering agreements keep their terms until their contracts expire. The result is that it now pays to use more of your own solar power on site — which puts more weight on batteries and on efficient buildings.

What this means for building design

  • Roofs: plan clear, shade-free areas, the right orientation, and safe access for cleaning and maintenance.
  • Structure: design for the weight of panels and mounting frames, and for wind loads.
  • Waterproofing: mounting penetrations are a common source of leaks if not detailed properly.
  • Electrical: space for inverters and batteries, proper earthing, and cable routes planned in advance.
  • Efficiency first: every unit of electricity saved by insulation and shading is one the panels do not need to produce.

Opportunities across the industry

Solar installers, inverter and battery suppliers, cable makers, roofing and waterproofing companies, and structural engineers all have a part in getting rooftop solar right. Generators, the solar industry, UPS systems and electrical cables are exhibitor categories at Build Asia. Read about the energy building code.

articles.title: Cement exports and new capacity: southern mills, African demand and US$700m of projects
articles.excerpt: Pakistan’s cement capacity reached 84.58 million tonnes in FY26 while exports shifted south and towards Africa. Where new capacity is coming from and what it means for suppliers.

sources.title: International Cement Review (CemNet), "Pakistan’s cement industry capacity reached 84.58Mt in FY26", 12 June 2026
Global Cement, "Update on Pakistan, July 2026", 8 July 2026
ProPakistani, "Cement sales rise 7% in September", 2 October 2026 (APCMA data)

articles.body:
Our analysis of FY26 cement despatches covered the strong year at home. This article looks at the other side of the industry: how much it can make, where its exports go and who is adding capacity.

Capacity and utilisation

According to the Pakistan Economic Survey 2025-26, as reported by CemNet in June 2026, installed cement capacity grew from 45.62 million tonnes in FY16 to 84.58 million tonnes in FY26. Utilisation improved to 60.2% from 55.1% a year earlier — so, by our calculation, about two-fifths of capacity is still idle. In July–March FY26, exports earned US$271 million, up 17.7% on both higher volumes and better prices.

Exports are moving south

Global Cement, citing AKD Research, reports that exports from northern mills fell after the Afghan border closed in late 2025 amid hostilities, while southern mills exported more on growing African demand. The first quarter of FY27 shows the split clearly:

July–September 2026 (APCMA)Million tonnesChange

articles.body:
Main Line-1 (ML-1) is Pakistan’s rail spine, running from Karachi to Peshawar. Upgrading it has been planned for years under CPEC. In 2026 the plan changed shape: the first section will start with multilateral money, and Chinese financing may follow later.

The financing as of 2026

  • Whole line: Dawn reported in July 2026 that the 1,680-km route was estimated at about $10 billion. Government figures reported by The Express Tribune in August 2026 gave about $6.66 billion for the “rationalised” project.
  • First phase: Dawn reported in July 2026 that the ADB had committed a loan package of around $2 billion. Profit reported in February 2026, when talks were at an advanced stage, that the ADB was expected to cover about $1.2 billion of the Karachi–Rohri section, with AIIB and the European Investment Bank in talks for the rest.
  • Preparation: The Express Tribune reported a $10 million ADB project readiness financing loan for Karachi–Rohri.
  • China: Dawn reported that starting with ADB money was judged prudent and that China had agreed; Mr Iqbal said Chinese financing could come in a later phase.

The timetable

What the works involve

The corridor is divided into five sections: Karachi–Rohri (480 km, estimated at $2.04 billion), Rohri–Multan, Multan–Lahore, Lahore–Rawalpindi and Rawalpindi–Peshawar. The planned works include:

  • rehabilitating the track and doubling it where needed;
  • better signalling and a higher axle load;
  • passenger train speeds of up to 160 km/h.

What this means for suppliers and partners

The following are observations. International competitive procurement under a multilateral lender usually opens work to qualified contractors and suppliers from many countries. Track materials, ballast, signalling, bridges and earthmoving fleets are all likely needs. Other rail plans, such as the proposed Reko Diq line, are covered separately.

articles.title: The Special Investment Facilitation Council explained: structure, sectors and projects
articles.excerpt: Set up in 2023 as a “single window” for investment, the SIFC coordinates federal and provincial bodies. How it is organised, what it has worked on, and the transparency questions.

sources.title: Board of Investment (invest.gov.pk), "Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC)", notification No. 7(218)-HR/2023
Radio Pakistan, "SIFC playing pivotal role in bringing investment to Pakistan", 7 May 2026
The News, "SIFC report to be made public by June 2027", 2 February 2026

articles.body:
The Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC) is often mentioned when large projects in Pakistan are announced. This is a plain guide to what it is and how it works.

What it is

The SIFC was constituted by the Prime Minister following a meeting on 2 June 2023 on attracting investment from Gulf (GCC) countries, through notification No. 7(218)-HR/2023. Its terms of reference include acting as a “Single Window” for cooperation with Gulf (GCC) and other countries, preparing a long-term investment roadmap, cutting bureaucratic hurdles, coordinating federal and provincial bodies, and fast-tracking projects. The original notification named five fields: defence, agriculture, minerals, IT and telecommunication, and energy.

How it is organised

TierMembers includeMeets
Apex CommitteePrime Minister, with federal ministers, provincial Chief Ministers and the Chief of Army Staff (by special invitation)Quarterly
Executive CommitteeMinister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives, federal and provincial ministers, provincial Chief SecretariesMonthly
Implementation CommitteeSIFC Secretariat, with sector coordinators and sectoral divisionsFortnightly

Officials from the Finance Ministry, the Board of Investment, the FBR and the State Bank are co-opted members, and a National Coordinator from the Pakistan Army sits on the Apex and Executive Committees.

What it has worked on

According to Radio Pakistan in May 2026, citing the Secretary of the SIFC Apex Committee, Dr Jahanzeb Khan, the council’s work has included:

  • Cement: facilitating the establishment of seven new cement factories. More on cement capacity.
  • Transport: logistics, railways and motorways, including reviving the M-12 motorway project.
  • Other sectors: large-scale farming, pharmaceuticals, warehousing and a medical tourism initiative.

Transparency

Following an IMF condition, the government has drawn up an action plan for the SIFC’s first annual report: a draft by December 2026, a final version by March 2027 and public release by June 2027. It is to list facilitated investments and the tax, policy and regulatory incentives granted, with a justification and estimated value for each.

What this means for the industry

For construction suppliers, the SIFC is mainly a signal of where large projects are being pushed, such as cement plants and transport. The annual report, once published, should give a clearer picture of what has actually been facilitated. See also: incentives in Special Economic Zones.

articles.title: Five numbers that shape Pakistan’s construction outlook for 2027
articles.excerpt: Growth, cement, housing need, mortgages and solar: five figures every builder, supplier and investor should keep in mind going into 2027.

sources.title: Asia News Network, "Pakistan economy grows 3.7pc in FY26 — fastest in four years, but short of target", 12 June 2026
Profit by Pakistan Today, "Cement dispatches rise 7.21% to 50.515 million tonnes in FY26", 4 July 2026
Business Recorder, opinion, 20 November 2025 (figures from PMRC, UN-Habitat and the ACASH Report 2023)
ProPakistani, "Pakistan's solar boom reaches 7,000 MW as govt moves to replace net metering", 17 July 2026

articles.body:
Forecasts come and go, but a handful of published figures explain most of what will happen in Pakistan’s building industry next year. Here are five worth keeping in view.

1. 5.73% — construction growth in FY26

The Economic Survey 2025-26 puts provisional construction growth at 5.73%, ahead of industry overall (3.51%). Read more on the survey figures.

2. 50.5 million tonnes — cement despatched in FY26

Total despatches rose 7.21%, and domestic sales 9.5%, to 41.5 million tonnes. Cement is the earliest hard signal of building activity. See the full breakdown.

3. About 1.06 million — new homes needed every year

Figures compiled from the Pakistan Mortgage Refinance Company, UN-Habitat and the ACASH Report put the annual increase in housing need at about 1.06 million units. In cities alone, about 350,000 new units are needed each year, but only around 150,000 are built. More on the housing gap.

4. 0.44% — mortgage finance as a share of GDP

The same sources put mortgage lending at just 0.44% of GDP. Most families still build or buy with savings, which keeps a large part of demand slow and incremental. Any growth in housing finance would change the pace of the market.

5. About 7,000 MW — rooftop solar under net metering

Net-metered solar grew from 190 MW in FY2020 to about 6,978 MW by FY2026, according to the Power Division’s energy adviser. Buildings are becoming power producers, which changes how roofs, wiring and structures are designed. How solar is reshaping building design.

Reading them together

The picture is of an industry growing again, with large unmet demand for homes, limited finance, and a fast shift towards energy-conscious buildings. Companies that offer affordable systems, faster building methods and energy-saving products are best placed for it.

articles.title: Heavy machinery on site: a safety checklist for contractors
articles.excerpt: Most machinery accidents are preventable. A practical daily checklist for site managers, operators and the people working around them.
articles.body:
Heavy machines make construction possible at scale — and they are behind many of the most serious accidents on building sites. Most of those accidents follow the same few patterns, which means most can be prevented with routine habits.

Before work starts each day

  • Walk-around inspection: tyres or tracks, hydraulic hoses, leaks, lights, mirrors, horn and reversing alarm.
  • Check the operator: trained and authorised for that machine, rested, and wearing the right protective equipment.
  • Check the ground: soft soil, slopes, trenches and buried services change what a machine can safely do.
  • Check overhead: power lines are a leading cause of fatal accidents with cranes, tippers and excavators.

Keep people and machines apart

  • Mark exclusion zones around working machines and lifting areas.
  • Use a trained banksman (signaller) whenever a machine reverses or visibility is limited.
  • Plan walkways so workers do not cross the machine’s path.
  • Never allow passengers or riding on buckets and forks.

Lifting operations

  • Know the load weight and the crane’s capacity at that radius — not just its maximum.
  • Inspect slings, chains and hooks before each lift.
  • Stop lifting in high wind.

Maintenance and records

Keep a service log for every machine and act on faults immediately. A machine that is “nearly fine” should not be on site. Lock out machines during maintenance so they cannot be started.

Build a safety culture

A short daily briefing, near-miss reporting without blame, and visible commitment from site management do more than any poster. Safety is also good business: accidents stop work, damage equipment and harm a company’s reputation.

Where it goes

In FY25 the United States (26.7%) and Germany (25.8%) together took more than half of exports. In the first seven months of FY26, Germany became the largest market at 27.5%, followed by the US (18.5%), the UK (16.7%), the UAE (8.6%) and Canada (3.0%).

What holds the sector back

  • Raw materials: forest cover is only about 5% of the country, and local timber supplies have been depleted. Makers increasingly use chipboard, metal and imported wood, which raises costs.

PACRA links furniture demand to residential and commercial construction, urbanisation and a growing middle class. Easier interest rates should help. articles.title: Light gauge steel framing: a faster way to build low-rise homes?
articles.excerpt: Light, termite-proof and quick to assemble, light gauge steel is being tested for affordable housing in Pakistan. How it works and where it fits.

sources.title: NED University of Engineering & Technology, Center for Affordable Housing and Sustainable Built Environment (CAHSBE), "Light Gauge Steel for Low Rise Buildings"

articles.body:
Most homes in Pakistan are built from brick, block and reinforced concrete — strong and familiar, but slow, heavy and labour-intensive. Light gauge steel (LGS) framing offers a different approach for low-rise buildings, and it is being studied seriously for affordable housing.

What it is

LGS framing uses thin, cold-formed steel sections — studs, joists and trusses — screwed together into wall and roof frames, then clad with boards and insulation. Sections are factory-made to exact sizes, so assembly on site is fast and precise.

The benefits

NED University’s Center for Affordable Housing and Sustainable Built Environment (CAHSBE) describes LGS as an attractive alternative to traditional reinforced concrete for low-rise buildings. It notes that:

  • sections are light enough to carry by hand, and allow quick building without heavy tools or equipment;
  • steel is non-combustible, which is a code requirement for some types of structures;
  • it does not rot, warp or suffer termite attack;
  • frames are easy to modify later.

Being tested in Pakistan

CAHSBE worked with the construction industry to build an affordable model house using LGS on the NED campus, and the university reports that LGS was considered as one of the technologies for the Naya Pakistan Housing initiative. Final-year engineering students at NED compare LGS designs with reinforced concrete alternatives for cost and time to completion.

Questions for anyone considering it

  1. Approvals: does the local building authority accept the system for this use?
  2. Corrosion: what galvanising and detailing protect the steel, especially near the coast?
  3. Heat and sound: what insulation and boards are used, and how does the home perform in summer?
  4. Skills: are trained installers available, and who supervises them?
  5. Cost: how does the full cost — including finishes — compare with a conventional build?

Light gauge steel framing has featured in Build Asia’s past conference programme, and pre-fabricated building components, pre-engineered steel buildings and prefab housing systems remain core exhibitor categories. Why faster building matters: the housing gap.

articles.title: Designing for heat: lessons from Karachi’s heatwaves
articles.excerpt: From 2015 to 2024, deadly heatwaves have shown how buildings and cities can trap heat. What architects, builders and planners can do about it.

sources.title: Dialogue Earth, "Karachi turns into heat trap", 24 June 2015
Bloomberg via BNN Bloomberg, "Karachi sees a surge in deaths as heat wave sears Pakistan", 27 June 2024

articles.body:
Karachi normally relies on its sea breeze, which the Pakistan Meteorological Department says keeps temperatures nearly 15°C lower than they would otherwise be. When that breeze fails during a heatwave, the city’s buildings and streets become part of the problem.

What the heatwaves showed

In June 2015 a heatwave lasting five to six days killed more than 750 people in the city, according to official reports at the time. In June 2024 Karachi reached 44°C, more than 7°C above normal, and the Edhi Foundation reported receiving 568 bodies over five days — far above its usual daily average — while officials disputed how many deaths were due to heat. The Sindh health department reported more than 2,100 heatstroke cases across the province that month. In both years, power cuts left many people without fans or cooling.

How cities trap heat

Experts quoted after the 2015 heatwave pointed to the way the city is built:

  • High-rise buildings closing natural wind corridors, according to urban planner Farhan Anwar;
  • concrete surfaces that absorb heat by day and release it at night, so the city cannot “breathe”;
  • too few trees to cool the air.

What design can do

  • Cool and green roofs: reflective coatings or planted roofs reduce heat entering top floors. Anwar proposed greening roofs and pointed to cities that now require roof gardens or solar panels.
  • Shading: deep window reveals, shades and verandas — features of traditional South Asian architecture.
  • Ventilation: orientation and openings that use the sea breeze, and layouts that keep air moving between buildings.
  • Insulation: keeps heat out, and keeps homes bearable during power cuts.
  • Trees and water: neem trees and revived natural drainage channels were among the measures suggested.

A shared responsibility

No single building fixes a city’s heat, but every building either adds to it or helps. Planners, architects, developers and material suppliers all have a part — and the same measures cut electricity bills, as the energy building code aims to do.

Insulation, reflective coatings, glazing and shading products are among the materials on show at Build Asia in Karachi.

articles.title: Exhibiting at Build Asia: shell scheme or bare space?
articles.excerpt: The two ways to take a stand, what each includes, and how to choose — plus tips for a stand that brings business.
articles.body:
Companies taking part in Build Asia choose between two kinds of stand. The right choice depends on what you are showing, your budget, and how you want to be seen.

Shell scheme: ready to use

A shell scheme stand is ready-built. The structure, fascia board with your company name, and basic furniture are supplied, so you arrive to a finished space and only need to bring products and graphics. Shell scheme starts at 9 square metres and increases in 9 m² steps (9, 18, 27 …).

Best for: first-time exhibitors, smaller products, distributors, service companies, and anyone who wants a simple, predictable setup.

Bare space: your own design

Bare space is floor area only. You design and build your own stand, usually with a contractor. Bare space starts at 18 square metres and increases in 9 m² steps (18, 27, 36 …).

Best for: established brands that want a distinctive presence, companies displaying large machinery, and anyone with a stand design they reuse across shows.

Both options include a 200-word company profile in the official exhibition catalogue. Heavy machinery can also be shown in the outdoor area.

Tips for a stand that brings business

  1. Set a goal: leads, distributors, launches or brand awareness — and design for it.
  2. Show, don’t just tell: working products, samples people can touch, and short demonstrations draw crowds.
  3. Keep the message short: visitors should know what you do from the aisle in three seconds.
  4. Staff it with decision-makers who can answer technical and commercial questions.
  5. Capture every lead with notes on what the visitor needs.
  6. Invite your customers before the show and give them a reason to come.
  7. Follow up within a week.

articles.title: Waterproofing before the monsoon: a checklist for owners and builders
articles.excerpt: Most leaks start at roofs, joints and wet areas. What to check, which systems to consider, and the questions to ask an applicator.
articles.body:
Water is the slowest and most expensive enemy of a building. Leaks damage plaster and paint, rust reinforcement inside concrete, and grow mould that affects health. Most problems start in a few predictable places — which means they can be prevented.

Where to look first

  • Roofs: cracks, ponding water, blocked drains, and the joint where roof meets parapet.
  • Bathrooms and kitchens: around drains, pipe entries and the base of walls.
  • Basements and water tanks: water pushing in from the soil or out from the tank.
  • External walls: hairline cracks, window and door frames, and where services enter the building.
  • Expansion joints in larger buildings, which need flexible sealants.

Common systems, in plain words

  • Cementitious coatings: brushed or troweled on; suit tanks, basements and wet areas.
  • Liquid membranes (acrylic, polyurethane): form a seamless flexible skin; suit roofs.
  • Bituminous membranes: sheets laid on roofs and foundations; durable but need careful laying.
  • Crystalline admixtures: added to concrete so it seals its own pores.
  • Sealants: for joints, frames and pipe entries.

Questions to ask an applicator

  1. How will the surface be prepared? Most failures come from poor preparation, not poor products.
  2. Is the system suited to our roof — exposed to sun, walked on, or covered?
  3. How thick will the coating be, and how many coats?
  4. What guarantee is given, and who gives it — the applicator or the manufacturer?
  5. Will you do a flood test on the roof before handing over?

Design it in from the start

The cheapest waterproofing is the one planned at design stage: proper roof slopes, enough drains, details at every joint, and good concrete. Repairs after leaks start always cost more.

  • What buyers want versus what the market offers — closing the gap between product and demand.

  • Design and structure.
